newsitem.title: USA: Critics say AIDS research biased against women.
newsitem.headline: Critics say AIDS research biased against women.

text.p: Some of the research work that has been applauded for extending the lives of thousands of AIDS patients came under attack on Wednesday for being biased in favour of men.
Doctors and AIDS activists at the National Conference on Women and HIV here said not enough research had considered how the disease manifests itself in women.

They said this bias could result in female AIDS sufferers being denied the same quality of life improvements their male counterparts were increasingly enjoying, and might even help explain some alarming data showing women were more likely than men to die of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome.

In 1996, for instance, the death rate among male AIDS patients fell 15 percent, but increased 3 percent in women. Statistics also show women were less likely to have access to the most advanced treatments available, and those who do may not respond as well as men because so many drugs are developed with male patients in mind.
"We still know very little about how the disease works in women's bodies," Mary Lucey, an AIDS policy analyst for Los Angeles said.
"I'd like to see the Food and Drug Administration include more women in the clinical research and have gender analysis before the approval of drugs."

Because there has been so little work on the gender differences of AIDS, researchers can only speculate how women's needs may differ. But they say there is sufficient medical information to make a case for studying the sexes separately. Women, for example, have dramatically different drug absorption rates than men and undergo hormonal changes during pregnancy and prior to menstruation that lead to immuno-suppression.

"We're in the middle of a revolution in HIV-related care," said Dr. Kathryn Anastos, an AIDS researcher from the Montefiore Medical Centre in New York, who also participated in the conference. "We now have treatments that can transform AIDS into a disease that can be managed over several decades, or potentially cured. But we are not getting (the treatments) to women as well as we are getting them to men."

The disparity may be explained partly by the fact that most AIDS patients are men. Of all AIDS cases diagnosed in the United States since officials started counting, about 57,000 have been men, and 13,000 women. That is changing with women accounting for more than 30 percent of all new AIDS cases.

Still, clinical trials of AIDS drugs have often included only a token woman or two. Despite some recent improvement, Lucey said the average AIDS drug study includes about 12 percent women. Along with focusing on how the drugs work in men, she said this practice can give male AIDS patients some of the best drugs years in advance.
